complaint_text: Complaint Against Goldman Sachs Bank USA Regarding Apple Card Monthly Installments, Misleading Balance Presentation, Credit Reporting Harm, and Refusal to Provide a Timely Remedy I am submitting this complaint against Goldman Sachs Bank USA, the issuer and credit-reporting furnisher for Apple Card, regarding the way Apple Card Monthly Installments are presented to consumers, reflected within the Apple Wallet interface, and subsequently reported to the consumer reporting agencies. This complaint is not based on a missed payment, delinquency, default, or failure to satisfy an account obligation. I have never been late on this account. My concern is that Goldman Sachs and Apple present Apple Card Monthly Installments as a low monthly payment arrangement while failing to prominently and meaningfully disclose that the entire remaining financed principal may be reported as revolving credit-card utilization, even though that full amount is not clearly reflected as the consumers current card balance or current payment obligation within the primary account display. This design is misleading, creates a foreseeable risk of substantial credit harm, and prevents consumers from making a fully informed decision about the financing product. Transaction and account history In XX/XX/year>, I purchased a MacBook Neo from Apple for approximately {$490.00} plus applicable sales tax. I specifically selected Apple Card Monthly Installments because the transaction was presented as an interest-free installment arrangement with a monthly payment of approximately {$41.00}. The Apple Card statement and primary account information presented the amount associated with the installment plan as a monthly obligation of {$41.00}. The full remaining installment principal was maintained separately within the Monthly Installments section rather than being clearly incorporated into the primary current card balance or payment amount displayed to me. Based on how the transaction and account balance were presented, I reasonably understood that the monthly installment would be the amount reflected as the current obligation associated with the financing arrangement. I was not provided with a sufficiently prominent warning at checkout, within the Wallet interface, or before the transaction was completed stating that : 1. The entire remaining financed balance would be reported to the credit bureaus as revolving credit-card utilization. 2. The amount reported to the credit bureaus could be substantially higher than the balance prominently displayed as currently due. 3. The resulting utilization increase could cause an immediate and significant credit-score reduction. XXXX. This could occur even when the account was fully current, the purchase was placed on a 0 % installment plan, and only a small monthly payment was due. On XX/XX/year>, Goldman Sachs reported an ending Apple Card balance of {$760.00} to XXXX That reported amount included the remaining financed purchase amount and other account activity, even though my statement reflected only the {$41.00} installment as the current installment payment. XXXX subsequently notified me that my credit score had decreased by XXXX points because of the reported increase in utilization. Immediate and serious mortgage-related harm This occurred while I was actively undergoing mortgage underwriting for the purchase of a home. Consumers are repeatedly instructed during the mortgage process not to open new accounts, incur substantial new debt, or materially increase credit-card balances. I intentionally selected the installment option because it was presented as a fixed monthly payment arrangement, and I believed that the credit impact would correspond to the stated monthly obligation. Instead, Goldman Sachs reported the full remaining financed amount as part of my revolving Apple Card balance without providing a prominent and understandable disclosure that this would occur. A XXXX credit-score decrease during active mortgage underwriting can affect : * Mortgage eligibility * Interest-rate qualification * Lender credits * Mortgage insurance * Debt and credit review requirements * Final underwriting approval * Closing conditions * The overall cost of borrowing The harm is not theoretical. I was required to notify my mortgage lender immediately and explain why my reported balance and credit score had unexpectedly changed during underwriting. I now face the possibility that the lender may require additional documentation, a credit supplement, a rapid rescore, or another credit review. I immediately paid the account in full As soon as I learned that Goldman Sachs had reported the full financed balance and that my score had decreased, I took immediate action. I paid the entire Apple Card balance in full, including : * The regular Apple Card balance * The remaining balance of the XXXX installment plan * Any other amount due on the account My Apple Card balance is now {$0.00}, and Apple has provided written confirmation showing that the current balance is {$0.00}. This was not a situation involving an inability or unwillingness to pay. Had the Apple Card interface clearly shown that the full installment principal would be reported as revolving utilization, or had it displayed the amount being furnished to the credit bureaus as the primary current card balance, I could have promptly paid the amount before the XX/XX/XXXX reporting date and avoided the damage. Instead, the product separated the amount currently presented as due from the much larger amount being treated as credit utilization for reporting purposes. Goldman Sachs refused to provide a meaningful remedy I contacted Goldman Sachs and opened case number XXXX to request assistance. I explained that : * The account was never delinquent. * The transaction was specifically placed on Apple Card Monthly Installments. * The statement reflected an installment payment of approximately {$41.00}. * Goldman Sachs reported a total balance of {$760.00}. * The reporting caused a XXXXXXXX XXXX score decrease. * I was actively undergoing mortgage underwriting. * I immediately paid the complete account and installment balance. * The current Apple Card balance is confirmed as {$0.00}. I requested that Goldman Sachs make a goodwill adjustment, provide an expedited or off-cycle update, or take another reasonable action to address the damage caused by this situation. Goldman Sachs representatives informed me that the company could not or would not make a goodwill adjustment or otherwise correct the reported balance before its normal reporting process. This response is inadequate. Goldman Sachs has been provided with documentation showing that the account is now paid in full and that the reported balance created an immediate risk to an active mortgage transaction. Nevertheless, Goldman Sachs has refused to provide a timely remedy or meaningful escalation. Telling a consumer to wait for a future reporting cycle is not a reasonable response when the financial harm is occurring now and may affect a time-sensitive mortgage approval. Deceptive and predatory effect of the installment structure I believe this practice is deceptive and predatory in effect. The product is marketed and presented around an affordable monthly installment. The consumer is shown the monthly amount due and is encouraged to view the transaction as a manageable, interest-free monthly obligation. However, the credit-reporting consequences are based on the entire remaining financed principal being treated as revolving credit utilization. The most important consequence of the financing arrangement is therefore not presented with the same prominence as the monthly payment being used to market the product. The consumer sees one amount as the current monthly obligation, while Goldman Sachs reports a substantially larger amount to the credit bureaus. That creates a material information imbalance. A reasonable consumer may believe that selecting a monthly installment option will result in the monthly installment being treated as the relevant monthly credit obligation. A consumer should not be expected to understand, without a prominent and specific disclosure, that the entire remaining financed amount will be reported as revolving utilization and could immediately reduce their credit score. The fact that the remaining installment principal may be located within a separate area of the Wallet application does not cure the problem. The interface should clearly display : * The amount currently due * The total remaining installment principal * The amount that may be reported as the credit-card balance * The effect the transaction may have on available credit and utilization * A clear warning that the full remaining amount may affect the consumers credit score This information should be presented before the consumer confirms the transaction, not discovered after the credit damage has occurred. Technical accuracy does not resolve the consumer-protection concern Goldman Sachs may respond that the reported amount was technically accurate because the remaining installment principal was owed under the Apple Card agreement. That response would not address the substance of this complaint. M y complaint concerns the material difference between : 1. How the product is marketed and presented to the consumer. 2. How the balance is displayed in the primary account interface. 3. What the consumer is told is currently due. 4. What Goldman Sachs reports as revolving credit utilization. 5. The absence of a clear warning about the foreseeable credit consequences. 6. Goldman Sachss refusal to provide an expedited remedy after the balance was paid in full. A practice may still be misleading or unfair when technically accurate information is presented in a manner that obscures a material consequence of the transaction. Consumers should not have to suffer a substantial credit-score reduction before learning how Goldman Sa chs reports Apple Card Monthly Installments. Requested investigation and resolution I request that the CFPB forward this complaint to Goldman Sachs Bank USA and require a substantive response addressing each issue raised. I specifically request that Goldman Sachs : 1. Conduct a formal investigation into the XX/XX/year> reporting of the {$760.00} balance. XXXX. Provide a detailed written breakdown of every amount included in the {$760.00} reported balance. XXXX. Identify the exact date the balance was furnished to XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX 4. Explain whether the entire remaining Apple Card Monthly Installment principal is reported as revolving credit utilization. 5. Identify the specific disclosure presented to me before checkout that clearly stated the full remaining financed amount would be reported as revolving utilization and could negatively affect my credit score. 6. Provide a copy of the version of that disclosure that was in effect on the purchase date. 7. Explain why the full amount being furnished to the credit bureaus was not displayed as the primary current Apple Card balance available for immediate payment before the reporting date. 8. Submit an immediate off-cycle update to XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX confirming that the account and installment balance are {$0.00}. 9. Where legally and operationally permissible, withdraw, revise, or otherwise correct the XX/XX/XXXX reporting so that the temporary installment balance does not continue to cause an inaccurate or misleading representation of my current credit utilization. 10. Provide written confirmation that the account was never delinquent, that no payment was missed, that the installment agreement was paid in full, and that the current account balance is {$0.00}. I need this documentation for my mortgage lender. 11. Confirm that no adverse, derogatory, disputed, or special comment code will be placed on the account in a manner that could create additional mortgage underwriting issues. 12. Review whether the Apple Card checkout process and Wallet interface clearly and conspicuously disclose the credit-reporting treatment of Monthly Installments. 13. Add a prominent pre-purchase warning advising consumers that the entire remaining financed amount may be reported as revolving credit utilization and may negatively affect their credit score. 14. Compensate me for any documented financial loss caused by this reporting, including increased mortgage pricing, lost lender credits, rapid-rescore expenses, delayed closing costs, or other direct damages. I am attaching or can provide the following supporting documentation : * Apple Card statement showing the {$41.00} installment * Apple Card Monthly Installment details * XXXX notification documenting the XXXX score decrease * Credit-report information showing the {$760.00} reported balance * Confirmation that the Apple Card balance is now {$0.00} * Confirmation that the installment plan was paid in full * Payment confirmation and bank records * Communications with Goldman Sachs * Goldman Sachs case information * Communications with my mortgage lender * Documentation of any resulting mortgage or financial impact I request a complete response rather than a generic statement that the information was reported accurately or that Goldman Sachs does not make goodwill adjustments. Goldman Sachs must address why the product prominently presents a small monthly installment while failing to give equally prominent notice that the full remaining financed principal may be reported as revolving utilization, and why it refuses to provide a timely remedy after the account has been paid in full and the consumer has documented immediate mortgage-related harm.

complaint_text: Statement of Fraud Victim Submitted to Wells Fargo Bank, CFPB, Office of the Comptroller, and the Arizona Attorney General 's Office My name is XXXX XXXX. I am XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, and a mortgage banking professional with XXXX years of experience in the financial industry. Throughout my career, I have completed annual training on fraud prevention, anti-money laundering laws, banking regulations, identity theft, and financial crimes. Despite that experience, I became the victim of one of the most sophisticated and psychologically manipulative fraud schemes I have ever encountered. This was not a simple scam. It was an elaborate impersonation of Wells Fargo 's Fraud Investigation Department that was so convincing it exploited my trust in the bank, my desire to protect my accounts, and my belief that I was assisting law enforcement in preventing a major financial crime. On the morning of XX/XX/XXXX, I received what appeared to be a legitimate Wells Fargo fraud alert via text message : " Wells Fargo Alert : Do you recognize {$1200.00} @ XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX Reply YES or NO. '' Since I had never made this purchase, I immediately replied " NO. '' Within moments, I received a second text message stating : " Free WF Msg : Thank you for your response. The attempted transaction is currently under review. A Wells Fargo representative will be contacting you shortly within about XXXX minutes. '' Shortly afterward, I received a phone call from an individual who identified himself as a member of the Wells Fargo XXXX XXXX XXXX. He spoke professionally, knew banking terminology, and immediately informed me that my accounts were under attack. He explained that criminals were attempting to use my accounts as part of a large money laundering operation and that Wells Fargo needed to immediately secure my accounts. As part of the " security process, '' he instructed me that Wells Fargo needed to verify my identity by sending authentication codes to my phone. Believing I was speaking with an actual Wells Fargo fraud investigator, I provided the requested authentication codes. What I did not realize until much later was that while I believed I was verifying my identity to Wells Fargo, I was actually giving the criminals the one-time security codes they needed to access my online banking, change my passwords, lock me out of my own accounts, and ultimately obtain unauthorized cash advances using my credit card accounts. The individual remained on the phone with me for more than two and a half hours. During that time, he never pressured me with threats or obvious scare tactics. Instead, he patiently answered every question I asked and consistently provided information that appeared to verify his identity and his access to confidential Wells Fargo systems. He told me my accounts had been identified in a federal money laundering investigation involving approximately one hundred Wells Fargo customers. According to him, criminals were using legitimate customer accounts to launder funds before withdrawing the money in person. He claimed I was one of ten customers currently being targeted. To reinforce the story, he sent me emails containing Wells Fargo logos and what appeared to be official documentation referencing cooperation between Wells Fargo, the FBI, and FinCEN in an ongoing money laundering investigation. Looking back, I now know these documents were fraudulent, but at the time they appeared authentic. Because I have spent my career in mortgage banking and have taken annual anti-money laundering training, I questioned nearly everything he told me. Every concern I raised was met with an immediate, detailed, and believable explanation. When I commented that I did not hear the normal Wells Fargo hold music whenever he placed me on hold, he explained that he was working from a secure investigation room with the FBI 's FinCEN division. That explanation seemed plausible given the nature of the investigation he described. He then instructed me to go to my local Wells Fargo branch because, according to him, an individual impersonating me was expected to return later that afternoon to withdraw approximately {$5600.00} in laundered funds from my account. He insisted that Wells Fargo needed me to withdraw the money first so federal investigators could use it as evidence in the criminal investigation. I initially refused and told him I would rather contact the police directly. Rather than becoming defensive, he calmly reassured me and continued providing details that, at the time, appeared impossible for anyone outside Wells Fargo to know. He instructed me to check my account balance at the Wells Fargo ATM before entering the branch. Before I even looked at the screen, he accurately stated the amount that was available in my account. When the ATM displayed the exact balance he had quoted, it significantly strengthened my belief that I was speaking with someone who had legitimate access to Wells Fargo 's internal systems. Once inside the bank, the deception became even more convincing. While I stood in line, the caller accurately identified the names of the tellers on duty and the branch manager. He told me I was third in line waiting to be served. He correctly described my clothing, including my blue shirt, white shorts, and the fact that I was wearing an earbud in my right ear. He even stated that he could see me through the bank 's surveillance cameras. At that point, I looked throughout the branch to determine whether anyone nearby could have been watching me. The branch was essentially empty, and there was no obvious way someone outside the bank could have observed me with such precision. Combined with his knowledge of my account information, this convinced me that he truly had access to Wells Fargo 's internal security systems. He then walked me through exactly what the teller would do before it happened. He predicted that she would ask whether I wanted large or small bills, that she would count the money twice using the counting machine, place the cash into an envelope, and provide me with a receipt bearing her name. Every one of those events occurred exactly as he described. Each correct prediction reinforced my belief that I was cooperating with a legitimate Wells Fargo fraud investigation rather than being manipulated by criminals. Looking back, I recognize these were carefully orchestrated psychological tactics designed to gain my trust. At the time, however, every piece of information the caller provided appeared to independently verify his legitimacy. That trust ultimately resulted in my being manipulated into surrendering {$5600.00} under the false belief that I was assisting Wells Fargo and federal investigators in stopping an active money laundering operation. The emotional impact of this crime has been devastating. Beyond the financial loss, I have experienced tremendous anxiety, humiliation, sleeplessness, and a profound loss of confidence in the very security systems I believed existed to protect customers. As someone who has spent nearly four decades in financial services helping others safeguard their finances, realizing that I had been manipulated so completely has been deeply traumatic. I respectfully request that Wells Fargo and the Arizona Attorney General fully investigate not only the fraud itself, but also how criminals were able to convincingly impersonate Wells Fargo personnel, possess information that appeared to come from internal banking systems, and manipulate a customer into believing he was acting under the direction of Wells Fargo and federal law enforcement. Wells Fargo 's Response and My Concerns Following the fraud, I immediately reported the incident to the XXXXXXXX XXXX XXXX. and Wells Fargo and fully cooperated with every request made by the Bank. I was assured that two separate fraud investigations would be opened and that the matter would be thoroughly investigated. Based on those assurances, I believed Wells Fargo would carefully review the circumstances surrounding this highly sophisticated fraud and objectively evaluate the evidence. Unfortunately, that was not my experience. Throughout this process, the bank never requested information from me regarding the case. They never asked for the police report, the text messages or the emails that caused me to fall victim to this fraud scheme. XXXX XXXX XXXX Department approached my claim as though I was responsible for what happened, rather than recognizing that I was the victim of an elaborate and well-orchestrated criminal scheme. At no point did I feel that my concerns were taken seriously or that the investigators demonstrated any empathy for the significant financial and emotional impact this crime has had on me. One of my greatest concerns is that there were numerous indicators of suspicious account activity that, in my opinion, should have triggered additional fraud prevention measures or, at a minimum, prompted immediate contact from the Bank. Within a very short period of time : My online banking password was changed multiple times. I was locked out of my own online banking account. Passwords associated with my credit card accounts were changed. Cash advances totaling approximately {$5600.00} were processed against my credit card accounts. These events were completely inconsistent with my normal banking behavior. I have been a loyal Wells Fargo customer for many years. During that time, I had never taken a cash advance against my credit cards, nor had I ever repeatedly changed my online banking passwords within minutes of one another. These activities represented a dramatic departure from my established account history. I repeatedly asked Wells Fargo representatives why these multiple password changes, account lockouts, and unusual cash advances did not generate heightened fraud alerts or additional verification procedures before the transactions were completed. To date, I have never received a meaningful explanation. Instead, Wells Fargo concluded that because I ultimately withdrew the money and handed it to criminals while acting under the false belief that I was assisting Wells Fargo and federal investigators, I had " received the benefit '' of the cash advances and was therefore solely responsible for repaying the {$5600.00}. I respectfully disagree with that conclusion. The fact that I physically withdrew the funds does not change the reality that I was deceived through criminal impersonation, social engineering, and fraudulent representations into surrendering those funds. I did not receive any benefit from this transaction. I was manipulated into acting under the belief that I was protecting my accounts and assisting Wells Fargo and law enforcement in an active fraud investigation. What has been equally disappointing has been Wells Fargo 's handling of my complaint after the initial report. I spoke with numerous representatives within Wells Fargo 's Executive Complaint Department who repeatedly assured me that they would keep me informed throughout the investigation and maintain communication with me. Those promises were never fulfilled. Instead, after long periods with little or no communication, I received form denial letters stating that Wells Fargo found no basis to approve my fraud claim and that I remained responsible for the entire {$5600.00} balance. There was no meaningful discussion of the extensive evidence I provided, no explanation addressing the specific concerns I raised regarding the suspicious activity on my accounts, and no indication that the sophisticated nature of this fraud had been seriously evaluated. As a result, I have been left feeling ignored, dismissed, and treated as though I was at fault simply because I became the victim of a highly sophisticated criminal enterprise. Because I believe this matter raises significant concerns regarding customer protection, fraud detection procedures, and the handling of fraud claims, I have sought assistance from every available regulatory and consumer protection agency. In addition to this complaint to the XXXXXXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, I have filed complaints with the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency ( XXXX ) and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau ( CFPB ). I have also sought assistance from XXXX 's XXXX XXXX XXXX and contacted local investigative reporters in the XXXX area in the hope that greater public awareness may help prevent other consumers from becoming victims of similar schemes. Finally, I am forwarding this complaint directly to the Executive Office of Wells Fargo, including Chief Executive Officer XXXX XXXX and the Board of Directors, because I believe senior leadership should be aware not only of the sophisticated fraud that occurred, but also of how my claim was handled after I reported it. My purpose in pursuing these complaints extends beyond recovering my financial loss. I want Wells Fargo to thoroughly examine whether its fraud detection systems, customer protections, and investigative processes are adequately protecting customers from increasingly sophisticated impersonation schemes. I also hope that my experience will lead to improvements that prevent other innocent customers from enduring the financial loss, emotional distress, and lasting impact that I continue to experience.
